{"id": "q73", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If the nine multi-seed BCI-middle retrains had not been run, which rung of the ladder could the study not populate at all, and which ablation finding could not have been observed?", "answer": "The 'reproducible latent code' rung could not be populated with any seed evidence, since all other settings use one seed. The finding that the group ordering on BCI middle depends on SAE seed could not have been observed, which removes one of the reasons for presenting ablations only descriptively.", "rubric": ["Identifies the reproducibility rung (consistency across seeds) as unpopulated.", "Identifies the seed dependence of the BCI-middle group ordering as unobservable."]},
{"id": "q74", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the clean-data exemplar inspection had used randomly chosen latents rather than latents selected by perturbation criteria, which of the paper's two lessons would no longer apply, and which would still apply?", "answer": "The caution to use quantities not involved in choosing the latents would no longer apply, because the selection would not depend on any perturbation-derived quantity. The bias of top-activation exemplars toward high-baseline latents would still apply, as would the weakness of conditioning on the activation extreme.", "rubric": ["States that the circularity concern (using quantities involved in selection) would no longer apply.", "States that the baseline-activity bias of exemplar views (conditioning on the extreme) would still apply."]},
{"id": "q75", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the depth-dependent loss of stability arises in the backbone representations themselves rather than in the SAEs fitted to them? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper measures stability only on sparse SAE codes, with a separate SAE trained at each depth. It does not measure how much the dense backbone activations change, so the decline cannot be attributed to the backbone or to the SAE.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that only SAE code overlap is measured, with separate SAEs per depth, and no dense-activation stability is reported."]},
{"id": "q76", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that high-baseline latents are intrinsically less interpretable than low-baseline latents? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper shows only that high-baseline latents dominate exemplar-based summaries because they are active on more trials, which is a selection bias of the method. It makes no claim about any latent's meaning.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that the finding concerns bias in exemplar summaries due to firing frequency, not the interpretability of those latents."]},
{"id": "q77", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that ablated latent groups carry little task information, given that ablation effects shrink after the probe is retrained? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The shrinkage is explained by the readout redistributing weight to correlated latents, so the information may be redundant rather than absent. Ablations test only whether a linear readout depends on a group, not what the group encodes. The paper explicitly draws no conclusion about task relevance.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that shrinkage reflects redistribution to correlated latents and that ablations test readout dependence only."]},
{"id": "q78", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that removing the alpha band changes the sparse codes more than removing other bands does? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The raw alpha response collapses once it is read against time-domain distortion, and the paper treats spectral responses as part of a code's general sensitivity to input change. It does not establish any alpha-specific dominance.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled (or not supported).", "Cites the collapse of the raw alpha response under distortion control and/or the reading of spectral responses as general sensitivity."]},
{"id": "q79", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that DINOv3's stronger depth effect is caused by its pretraining on another modality? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Only one vision backbone is tested, with one seed per setting. DINOv3 also differs in input format (channel-by-time images) and uses reduced dictionary width on BCI and MA, so modality is confounded with other differences.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Names at least one confound, such as the single vision model, reduced dictionary width, different input format or single seed."]},
{"id": "q80", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the depth-dependent stability decline holds for SAEs with other sparsity levels or training objectives? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Every dictionary is a TopK SAE with k=32 trained with MSE plus AuxK. No other k, ℓ1 penalty or architecture is tested.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Explains that only TopK with k=32 (MSE plus AuxK) was tested."]},
{"id": "q81", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the late-minus-early Jaccard decrease is statistically reliable within each individual backbone–dataset combination? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Each combination has a single SAE seed (apart from BCI middle), and the bootstrap resamples settings to give pooled intervals, not per-combination ones. The 9/9 count shows a consistent sign but not per-combination reliability.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Cites single seeds per combination and/or that bootstrap intervals are pooled over settings rather than computed per combination."]}
]}

{"items": [
{"id": "q1", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the paper normalize each block's token activations to E||x||=√d before mixing consecutive blocks into one layer group for SAE training?", "answer": "Each layer-group SAE is trained with reconstruction MSE on tokens pooled from several blocks. If those blocks differed in activation scale, the high-norm blocks would dominate the loss, and the dictionary would mostly fit them. Normalizing first puts every block on a common scale, so the group dictionary reflects all its blocks and reconstruction/FVU is comparable across groups and backbones.", "rubric": ["States that normalization prevents blocks with larger activation norms from dominating the group dictionary (or makes blocks contribute comparably).", "Reason: the SAE is fit by MSE on mixed tokens, so errors on larger-scale tokens weigh more in the loss.", "Optionally notes that it makes reconstruction/FVU comparable across layer groups or backbones."]},
{"id": "q2", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why do pooled selectivity and importance summaries over the 21 task-analysis settings mostly reflect CBraMod and DINOv3 rather than all three backbones equally?", "answer": "REVE's MA and Speech exports were unavailable, so REVE contributes only its 3 BCI settings. CBraMod and DINOv3 contribute 9 settings each. Because the bootstrap resamples settings with equal weight, REVE makes up only about 1/7 of the pool.", "rubric": ["States that REVE is underrepresented (3 of 21 settings, BCI only).", "Reason: REVE MA/Speech task-readout exports were missing, and the bootstrap weights each setting equally."]},
{"id": "q3", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the activity-matching procedure pick controls by squared z-distance on standardized firing rate and mean activation rather than by raw differences?", "answer": "Firing rate and mean activation are on different numerical scales. An unstandardized distance would be dominated by whichever quantity has the larger range, so matching would effectively ignore the other. Z-scoring on the union of selected and candidate latents makes both count comparably.", "rubric": ["States that standardization lets both quantities contribute comparably to the match.", "Reason: the two quantities have different scales, so a raw distance would be dominated by one of them."]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the alpha test compare the 8–12 Hz notch against a width-matched 30–34 Hz sham rather than only against the clean trial?", "answer": "Band-stops alter sparse codes in every backbone, so any notch will move the code relative to the clean trial. A clean-only comparison cannot separate an alpha-specific response from generic sensitivity to removing a 4 Hz band. A sham of equal width gives a baseline for that generic notch effect.", "rubric": ["States that the sham provides a baseline for the generic effect of applying a band-stop of the same width.", "Reason: band-stops change codes in every backbone, so a change relative to clean alone does not show alpha specificity."]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does reporting that the late-minus-early Jaccard decrease occurs in 9/9 combinations add information beyond the pooled means of -0.17 and -0.20?", "answer": "A pooled mean could be driven largely by DINOv3's large decline (about -0.35). The 9/9 count shows the decline is present in every backbone–dataset combination, including REVE's mild ones. So the depth effect is not an artifact of one backbone dominating the average.", "rubric": ["States that the count shows the decline is consistent across all combinations rather than driven by a few.", "Reason: the mean could be dominated by DINOv3's large effect while other backbones (e.g., REVE at about -0.07) are small."]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why are activity-matched controls drawn from the same dictionary, with matching applied within each dictionary before pooling, rather than from a shared pool of latents across settings?", "answer": "Firing rates and activation scales depend on the dictionary, which differs by backbone, layer, dataset and width. Latents are also evaluated on that dictionary's own trials and compete under its TopK. Matching across dictionaries would confound the selected-versus-control difference with differences between settings.", "rubric": ["States that within-dictionary matching keeps the setting fixed so the comparison isolates selected versus control latents.", "Reason: activity statistics and competition differ across dictionaries/settings, so cross-dictionary matching would mix in setting differences."]},
{"id": "q7", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the random-versus-contiguous dropout comparison carried out with a matched number of zeroed channels?", "answer": "Zeroing more channels is a larger input change (larger time-domain distortion) and would by itself lower Jaccard. Matching the count holds the amount of removed input roughly constant. Any remaining difference can then be attributed to spatial adjacency rather than to the size of the perturbation.", "rubric": ["States that matching isolates the effect of adjacency/spatial arrangement.", "Reason: more zeroed channels means a larger input change that would reduce stability on its own."]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c4", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "The stability rung uses perturbations that should not change the underlying signal content much. When would a low Jaccard under contiguous channel dropout not count against a latent's stability, and why?", "answer": "It would not count against the latent when the zeroed neighborhood carries the very signal content the latent represents. In that case the perturbation genuinely changes the content, so a changed code is appropriate rather than a sign of instability. The rung's premise of a content-preserving perturbation would be violated.", "rubric": ["Identifies the case where the dropped channels/region contain the information the latent encodes.", "Reason: the perturbation then changes the underlying content, violating the rung's assumption, so a code change is expected."]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "In a setting where the logistic probe's balanced accuracy is at chance, would importance scores and group-ablation effects say anything about how the readout depends on task information?", "answer": "No. A chance-level probe has captured no task structure, so its weights, and hence |w_j|E_train[c_j], describe an uninformative readout. Ablations cannot meaningfully lower accuracy from chance either. This is one reason the paper compares ablations only within settings, given the 0.236–0.625 accuracy span.", "rubric": ["Concludes that importance and ablations would be uninformative in that setting.", "Reason: the probe has learned no task structure, so its weights and accuracy drops carry no task-dependence information."]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Appendix B pools the alpha/sham contrast by backbone over its nine dataset–depth settings. When would this pooling hide a genuine alpha-specific response?", "answer": "Pooling would hide the response if it were present only in one dataset or at one depth. That is plausible because code sensitivity changes strongly with depth. Averaging such a setting with eight settings that lack the response would dilute it toward the generic response.", "rubric": ["Identifies the case where the response is confined to a subset of datasets or depths.", "Reason: pooling over nine settings averages it with settings lacking the response; code sensitivity is known to vary with depth."]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "When would a high early-layer active-set Jaccard under channel dropout overstate how stable the code is?", "answer": "It would overstate stability if the active sets were dominated by high-baseline latents that fire on almost every token regardless of input. Those latents stay active in both the clean and perturbed codes and keep Jaccard high, even if the input-dependent latents are swapped. The paper documents that latents differ strongly in baseline activity.", "rubric": ["Identifies always-on or high-baseline latents occupying many of the active slots.", "Reason: such latents remain active under any perturbation and inflate the overlap even when the input-dependent latents change."]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose a selected latent and its control are matched on clean firing rate and mean activation as in Appendix A. When would comparing their top-five clean exemplars still be biased?", "answer": "The comparison would still be biased when the two latents have different activation tails, for example when one is heavy-tailed. Top-five exemplars condition on the extreme of the activation distribution, which firing rate and mean activation do not constrain. Matched latents can therefore still yield systematically different exemplars.", "rubric": ["Identifies a difference in the upper tail or shape of the activation distribution despite matched rate and mean.", "Reason: exemplars condition on the activation extreme, which the matching variables do not control."]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "The paper models electrode failure by zeroing channels in the raw signal. Would its dropout Jaccard results reliably describe deployments where a failing electrode outputs large-amplitude noise instead of zeros?", "answer": "Not reliably. Only zeroing was tested. A noisy channel adds spurious signal rather than removing it and can produce a much larger input change, so code stability under that failure mode could differ, likely being worse, and remains untested.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the results do not reliably transfer to noisy-electrode failures.", "Reason: only channel zeroing was tested, and a noise channel is a different (possibly larger) input change."]},
{"id": "q14", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Assume both the clean and perturbed codes of a token have all k=32 TopK latents active. What active-set Jaccard corresponds to exactly 16 of the clean active latents remaining active after perturbation?", "answer": "The intersection is 16 and the union is 32+32−16 = 48. The Jaccard is therefore 16/48 = 1/3, about 0.33.", "rubric": ["Gives a Jaccard of 1/3 (about 0.33).", "Reason: with both sets of size 32 and 16 shared, the union is 48."]},
{"id": "q15", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A team can afford three-seed retraining in only two more CBraMod settings to test whether its BCI depth decline is reproducible across seeds. Which settings should they retrain, and why?", "answer": "They should retrain BCI early and BCI late. The depth claim is a late-minus-early contrast, and both endpoints currently have a single seed. BCI middle already has three seeds and does not enter that contrast.", "rubric": ["Chooses the BCI early and BCI late settings.", "Reason: the depth contrast uses early and late, which have only one seed; middle is already multi-seed and not part of the contrast."]},
{"id": "q16", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A researcher selects the latents with the highest probe importance and inspects their top-activating clean exemplars. What bias should they expect, and what does the paper recommend to counter it?", "answer": "Importance is |w_j|E_train[c_j], so it favours latents with high mean activation, that is, high-baseline latents. These are exactly the latents that dominate exemplar summaries. The researcher should compare against controls matched in firing rate and mean activation, and prefer correlational summaries over all trials.", "rubric": ["States that the selection is biased toward high-baseline latents.", "Reason: the importance score includes the E_train[c_j] factor, and high-baseline latents dominate exemplar views.", "Recommends activity-matched controls (and/or all-trial correlational summaries)."]},
{"id": "q17", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to rank CBraMod, REVE and DINOv3 by how much their codes lose stability with depth under random (not contiguous) channel dropout, using only the paper's reported numbers. Can they?", "answer": "No. The per-backbone late-minus-early contrasts are reported only for contiguous dropout. Random dropout is given only as the pooled mean of -0.17 across all nine combinations.", "rubric": ["Concludes that they cannot rank the backbones under random dropout from the reported numbers.", "Reason: per-backbone values are given only for contiguous dropout; random dropout is reported only as a pooled mean."]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A team trains TopK SAEs with k=64 on a new EEG model and wants to use the paper's FVU range [0.059, 0.228] as the benchmark for passing rung 1. Is that a valid comparison?", "answer": "No. The paper's range is measured at L0=32, and rung 1 is defined as low reconstruction error at fixed sparsity. A dictionary allowed twice as many active latents is not reconstructing under the same constraint. They need to compare at matched L0, or report their own sparsity explicitly.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the comparison is not valid as is.", "Reason: rung 1 and the paper's FVU range are defined at a fixed sparsity (L0=32), and sparsity affects reconstruction."]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A group runs the alpha (8–12 Hz) versus 30–34 Hz sham test on recordings where 30–34 Hz power far exceeds 8–12 Hz power, and finds that codes change more under the sham. How should this be read under the paper's distortion logic?", "answer": "In these recordings the sham removes more energy, so its time-domain distortion is larger than the alpha notch's. The larger code change may reflect that larger input change rather than any band-specific response. Responses must be compared relative to each perturbation's distortion before reading them.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the larger sham response does not by itself indicate 30–34 Hz specificity.", "Reason: the sham produces the larger time-domain distortion here, so responses must be read alongside distortion."]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If the raw alpha response had survived distortion control, which rung would that result bear on, and what in the paper would still block naming latents 'alpha'?", "answer": "It would feed the descriptive band-wise response profile, the top rung. Naming would still be blocked for several reasons:\n- That rung presupposes stability and reproducibility, which are depth-dependent and mostly single-seed.\n- Clean-data inspection did not support band-specific names.\n- Band-stops cannot isolate a biological oscillator.\n- The ladder never certifies meaning.", "rubric": ["Identifies the descriptively profiled latent (band-wise profile) rung.", "Gives at least one paper-based reason naming remains unjustified (lower rungs not secured, clean-data validation failed, band-stops cannot isolate an oscillator, or the ladder does not certify meaning)."]},
{"id": "q21", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the depth decline in Jaccard had appeared under contiguous dropout but not under random dropout, which reported statement would no longer hold as written?", "answer": "The statement that late-layer overlap is lower than early-layer overlap for both random and contiguous dropout in all nine combinations would fail. That statement includes the pooled random-dropout mean of -0.17. The depth claim would then be limited to spatially clustered dropout.", "rubric": ["Names the claim that the depth decline holds for both random and contiguous dropout across combinations (random mean -0.17).", "Reason: the hypothetical removes the random-dropout decline, restricting the effect to contiguous dropout."]},
{"id": "q22", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If code cosine between clean and channel-dropped codes had stayed near 1 at every depth while active-set Jaccard fell with depth, what would that imply about the nature of the depth effect?", "answer": "The active-set changes would then involve latents with small activations near the TopK cutoff, a form of rank displacement, while the dominant code content was preserved. The depth effect would amount mostly to marginal membership swaps. That would weaken the deployment concern about deep codes.", "rubric": ["States that the swaps would involve low-magnitude, near-cutoff latents, so the main code content is preserved.", "Reason: high cosine despite changed membership means the swapped latents carry little of the code's magnitude."]},
{"id": "q23", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the latent groups chosen by perturbation criteria had turned out matched in baseline activity, which reasons for presenting the group ablations only descriptively would remain?", "answer": "Two reasons would remain. Ablation effects shrink after probe retraining, because the readout can redistribute weight to correlated latents. And the group ordering on BCI middle depends on the SAE seed. Relevance would also still be defined only for a logistic probe on mean-pooled codes.", "rubric": ["Names shrinkage of effects after probe retraining as a remaining reason.", "Names seed dependence of the BCI-middle group ordering as a remaining reason (mentioning the logistic/mean-pooled scope is optional)."]},
{"id": "q24", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the recorded time-domain distortion of contiguous dropout had been consistently larger than that of random dropout with the same number of channels, which interpretation would weaken, and why?", "answer": "The local scalp-neighborhood pooling interpretation of why contiguous dropout is more damaging would weaken. The extra damage could instead be explained simply by a larger input change, without appealing to how representations pool over adjacent channels.", "rubric": ["Identifies the local-pooling interpretation of contiguous dropout's greater damage.", "Reason: a larger input change would offer an alternative explanation for the extra code disruption."]},
{"id": "q25", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c3", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If the depth decline had appeared only for DINOv3, with flat Jaccard across depth for CBraMod and REVE, which claim would lose its support?", "answer": "The claim that deeper SAE codes are less stable in both EEG-native and cross-modal backbones, including the 9/9 count, would lose support. The recommendation to report layer as a primary variable for EEG foundation models would then rest only on the cross-modal backbone.", "rubric": ["Names the claim that the depth decline holds in EEG-native as well as cross-modal backbones (or the 9/9 count).", "Reason: the EEG-pretrained backbones would no longer show the decline, so the generality to EEG foundation models fails."]},
{"id": "q26", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that CBraMod's final block (block 11) yields less dropout-stable SAE codes than its first block (block 0)? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Dictionaries are trained on layer groups that mix blocks 0–3 and 8–11 after normalization. Stability is therefore measured per group, with no per-block measurement.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: SAEs and stability are computed on mixed multi-block layer groups, not on individual blocks."]},
{"id": "q27", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Do the paper's bootstrap confidence intervals quantify how its stability summaries would change under a different train/test split? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled; the intervals do not capture this. Splits are fixed, and the intervals resample settings. They therefore reflect only variability between settings, not variability due to the choice of split.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled (the intervals do not capture split variability).", "Reason: splits are fixed and the bootstrap resamples settings only."]},
{"id": "q28", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that linear probes on late-layer pooled codes lose more balanced accuracy under channel dropout than probes on early-layer codes? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Stability is measured as Jaccard and cosine on the codes. The probe analyses use clean codes with latent-group ablations, not perturbed inputs. Mean pooling could also absorb token-level swaps, and no probe accuracy under dropout is reported.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: dropout effects are measured on code overlap, not on probe accuracy under perturbed inputs (probes and ablations use clean data)."]},
{"id": "q29", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that vision foundation models are unsuitable for EEG classification? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted as far as the paper goes. DINOv3 encodes EEG usefully for downstream linear probes. What the paper finds is that its deep codes are the least robust to channel dropout, a separate property. Only one vision model was tested.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted (not supported).", "Reason: DINOv3 transfers usefully to EEG probes; the deficit is in internal robustness, which is reported as a separate property."]},
{"id": "q30", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper support that the depth-dependent dropout instability holds across EEG datasets that differ in channel count and paradigm? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Supported within its range. The decline appears in 9/9 combinations spanning BCI (22-channel motor imagery), MA (20-channel workload) and Speech (64-channel imagined speech). Datasets beyond these remain untested.", "rubric": ["Answers supported (within the studied datasets).", "Reason: the decline holds in all combinations across three datasets with 20, 22 and 64 channels and distinct paradigms."]},
{"id": "q31", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that its SAE codes are stable when the montage changes, for example a different electrode layout or channel count between recordings? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Montage variation appears only as motivation. The perturbations zero channels within each dataset's fixed montage, and dictionaries are trained per dataset, so cross-montage stability was never measured.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: only channel zeroing within fixed per-dataset montages was tested; montage changes were not."]},
{"id": "q32", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that every individual latent is less stable in late-layer dictionaries than in early-layer ones? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The reported quantities are mean active-set Jaccard and code cosine per setting, with intervals over settings rather than latents. These set-level averages say nothing about each individual latent's behavior.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: stability is summarized as set-level means per setting (bootstrapped over settings), not as per-latent comparisons across layers."]},
{"id": "q33", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Could code cosine between a clean and a perturbed sparse code fall below 1 while active-set Jaccard remains exactly 1?", "answer": "Yes. The same 32 latents can stay active while their magnitudes change. That leaves Jaccard at 1 but makes the codes non-parallel, so cosine drops below 1.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Reason: Jaccard depends only on which latents are active, while cosine also reflects activation magnitudes."]},
{"id": "q34", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Could active-set Jaccard between a clean and a perturbed sparse code fall below 1 while code cosine remains exactly 1?", "answer": "No. Codes are nonnegative because of the ReLU. Different active sets mean some coordinate is positive in one code and zero in the other, so the two vectors cannot be parallel and cosine must be below 1.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Reason: with nonnegative codes, a change in support makes the vectors non-parallel, so cosine drops below 1."]},
{"id": "q35", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Within one backbone and dataset, would accounting for time-domain distortion change how the alpha-notch response compares with the 30–34 Hz sham response?", "answer": "Yes. The two equal-width notches remove different amounts of signal energy, so their distortions differ. Reading responses alongside distortion is exactly what makes the raw alpha response collapse.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Reason: the alpha and sham band-stops produce different time-domain distortions on the same trials."]},
